title: 'Zombie' cells may drive common form of epilepsy | Live Science
abstract: Scientists are unraveling the role of senescent cells in a common form of epilepsy, and it could point to new treatments. Destroying "undead" cells in the brain may help to relieve a common form of epilepsy, a new lab study suggests. In the research, published in the journal Annals of Neurology, researchers found that clearing away damaged-but-undying brain cells in mouse models of epilepsy improved the rodents' memory and reduced their number of seizures. In their new paper, Forcelli and his colleagues asked whether removing senescent cells from the brain might alter the symptoms of TLE. Next, in mouse models of TLE, the team showed that the animals also had more signs of senescence in their brains than did mice without seizures. These signs of senescence were most strongly linked to microglia, cells that form part of the brain's in-house immune system. James Kirkland, a gerontologist at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center who first identified the two compounds' senolytic effects, told Live Science that they target the pathways that senescent cells use to resist normal cell death.
